lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. Saturday, 5 p.m., the void deck of Block 208.
**Mum:** Kavya! Paati turns **64** today. Party at six. Everything gets shared **equally**.
**Paati:** Equally? I'm the birthday girl. I want the **biggest** slice.
**Dad:** Relax. For any number problem I have one rule: **just multiply them**.
**Kavya:** Dad, that's not a rule. That's a hobby.
**Narrator:** But this documentary is about the most exclusive club in Singapore. Behind the third pillar.
**Big Two:** Big Two. Security, **the Prime Club**. Members have **exactly two factors**: 1 and themselves.
**Big Two:** I'm the only **even** prime. Every other even number has **me** as a factor. Not on the list.
**One:** Hi! I'm **One**! Can I come in? I'm a factor of **every** number!
**Big Two:** You've got **one** factor. Exactly **two**, or you're **not on the list**.
**One:** Okay! I'll try again later!
**Narrator:** Prime Time. Episode 2: Paati Turns Sixty-Four.
**Narrator:** 5:15 p.m. **36** plastic chairs. Mum wants a perfect **rectangle**.
**Ah Boy:** Five rows! Five is my lucky number!
**Kavya:** 36 ÷ 5 = 7 remainder **1**. 5 is **not** a factor of 36.
**One:** A leftover one? That's me! Hi!
**Big Two:** A **factor** divides **exactly**. Find them in **pairs**, starting at 1.
**Big Two:** The pairs have **met**. Stop. After that they just swap round.
**Paati:** **Six by six**, please. A square. Squares are classy.
**Big Two:** **Multiples** of 36? 36, 72, 108... **forever**. **Factors fit in. Multiples make more.**
**Priya:** Priya. Best friend. My family's coming: **23** people. Make them a rectangle!
**Kavya:** 23 chairs: only **1 × 23**. One long line.
**Big Two:** Exactly two factors: **1** and **itself**. **23 is prime.** Welcome to the club.
**Big Two:** 36 has more than two: **composite**. One has one factor: **neither**.

chapters.title: At the door of the Prime Club

lines.cap: **Narrator:** 6 p.m. The guests arrive. So do the numbers.
**Priya:** Easy rule: **all odd numbers are prime**. Let them all in!
**Big Two:** 9 = 3 × 3. 15 = 3 × 5. 21 = 3 × 7. **Odd, but composite.** Not on the list.
**Priya:** Fine. **91** is definitely prime. Look at it!
**Big Two:** Test the primes **2, 3, 5, 7**... Stop when the next prime **squared** is **bigger** than the number.
**Kavya:** 11² = 121 is too big, so stop at 7. And 91 ÷ 7 = **13**. **Composite!**
**Mr Tan:** Good evening. **Mr Tan**, seventh floor. Kavya's maths teacher. Happy birthday, Paati.
**Mr Tan:** A jigsaw: **7452** pieces. Can the tables share it **equally**?
**Kavya:** **4** tables? Check the **last two** digits: 52 = 4 × 13. **Yes.**
**Priya:** No! 7 + 4 + 5 + 2 = 18, and 18 isn't a multiple of 4!
**Mr Tan:** The **digit sum** only works for **3** and **9**. For 2, 4, 8, check the **last 1, 2, 3** digits.
**Kavya:** Digit sum 18: so **3** and **9** work. Even too, so **6** works. 8? 452 = 8 × 56 + 4. **No.**
**Mr Tan:** Why was 6 afraid of 7? Because 7, 8, 9.
**Paati:** Seven **ate** nine? Not at a vegetarian party.
**Narrator:** 6:30 p.m. Kavya, Priya and Ah Boy hang **120** fairy lights on the old banyan tree.
**Banyan:** Hmmm. I am **Banyan**. I split things. Slowly.
**Banyan:** Split 120 **any** way you like. Keep splitting until every branch ends in a **prime**.
**Priya:** 8 × 15. That's 2 × 2 × 2 and 3 × 5. Done first!
**Ah Boy:** 2 × 60! Then 6 × 10, then 2 × 3 and 2 × 5!
**Kavya:** We all got **2, 2, 2, 3** and **5**.
**Banyan:** Every whole number above 1 has **exactly one** prime factorisation. Its **DNA**.
**Banyan:** In **index form**, smallest prime first: **120 = 2³ × 3 × 5**.
**Mum:** My turn. I made **180** laddoos for Paati.
**Banyan:** The **ladder**: divide by the **smallest** prime that fits, until you reach **1**.
**Banyan:** **15** isn't prime. Split it: **180 = 2² × 3² × 5**.
**Mum:** Multiply back: 4 × 9 × 5 = **180**. Every laddoo accounted for.
**Narrator:** 6:45 p.m. Mum brought **60** cups. Dad brought **72** plates. They are not speaking.
**Mum:** The **most** tables, all set the same. I **listed** both sets of factors: the highest common one is **12**. It took ten minutes.
**Hattie:** Hattie! She's **Lottie**. We're a **Venn diagram**: faster for big numbers.
**Lottie:** Don't touch my side.
**Hattie:** Prime factors first. **60 = 2² × 3 × 5**.
**Lottie:** And **72 = 2³ × 3²**.
**Hattie:** Shared primes go in the **middle**: **2, 2, 3**. Leftovers stay home: my **5**, her **2** and **3**.
**Lottie:** **HCF**: multiply the middle. 2 × 2 × 3 = **12**. **HCF is the Heart.**
**Kavya:** So **12** tables, each with **5** cups and **6** plates.
**Hattie:** **LCM**: multiply the **lot**. 5 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 2 × 3 = **360**. **LCM is the Lot.**
**Lottie:** From index form: HCF takes the **lows**, 2² × 3. LCM takes the **highs**, 2³ × 3² × 5.
**Dad:** Small numbers, my way. LCM of 6 and 8? **Just multiply them**: 48!
**Priya:** **List** the multiples of 8: 8, 16, **24**. 6 goes into 24. **LCM = 24.** They **share** a 2!
**Dad:** Four and nine, then. 4 × 9 = **36**!
**Kavya:** They share **no** primes, so the LCM **is** 36. Dad... you're right.
**Dad:** I've never been right before. I don't know what to do with my hands.
**Narrator:** 7 p.m. Paati's sisters are on two buses: one every **12** minutes, one every **18**.
**Paati:** Both buses left at seven. When do they next leave **together**?
**Big Two:** First question at my door: are we **building up**, or **breaking down**?
**Kavya:** 12, 24, **36**. 18, **36**. **Building up**: multiples. The **LCM**: 36.
**Ah Boy:** So the answer is **36**!
**Big Two:** The question asked **when**. Seven o'clock plus 36 minutes: **7:36 p.m.**
**Dad:** My fairy lights flash every **8** and every **12** seconds. Together every 8 × 12 = **96**!
**Big Two:** They flash together every **24**: LCM = 2³ × 3 = **24**. 96 is **a** common multiple, not the **lowest**.
**Dad:** Veggie burgers come in packs of **6**, buns in packs of **8**. I bought eight packs and six packs!
**Mum:** **Fewest** packs: LCM(6, 8) = **24**. So **4 packs** of burgers, **3 packs** of buns.
**Ah Boy:** Goodie bags! **36** chocolate coins, **48** lollipops. Most identical bags: **48**!
**Big Two:** **Breaking down** into equal groups, nothing left over: **HCF**.
**Kavya:** HCF(36, 48) = **12**. So **12** bags, each with **3** coins and **4** lollipops.
**Big Two:** Sense check: an **HCF** is at most the **smaller** number. An **LCM** is at least the **bigger**.
**Paati:** Seven thirty-six. Same bus, same time. Now they'll have to talk to each other.
**Narrator:** 7:45 p.m. Cake time. Paati asked for **64** cupcakes.
**Cubert:** **Cubert!** A **cube**! Sixty-four is **my** number!
**Mum:** On a tray, it's **8 by 8**: 8² = 64. A **square**.
**Cubert:** Or a tower, **4 by 4 by 4**: 4³ = 64. A **cube**!
**Paati:** A square **and** a cube. I am **perfect**.
**Mr Tan:** Technically, a **perfect number** is the sum of its other factors. Like **6** = 1 + 2 + 3.
**Paati:** Technically, it's my birthday.
**Cubert:** **64 = 2⁶**. Squares have **even** powers. Cubes have powers in the **3** times table.
**Cubert:** **Square root**: halve every power: 2³ = **8**. **Cube root**: divide every power by 3: 2² = **4**.
**Mr Tan:** Quick one. What's **√1764**?
**Ah Boy:** Half of 1764 is **882**!
**Cubert:** Halve the **powers**, not the number! 1764 = 2² × 3² × 7².
**Mum:** My **180** laddoos won't make a square. 180 = 2² × 3² × **5**.
**Cubert:** Only the **5** has an **odd** power. × 5: 180 × 5 = **900 = 30²**.
**Ah Boy:** Or **÷ 5**: keep **36**, a 6 by 6 square. I eat the other **144**.
**Cubert:** A **cube**? Every power to a multiple of 3: × 2 × 3 × 5² = **150**. **27 000** laddoos!
**Mum:** Square tray. Seven hundred and twenty more laddoos it is.
**Narrator:** 8 p.m. Mr Tan has brought a party quiz. Nobody asked him to.
**Mr Tan:** How many factors does **72** have? **Without** listing them.
**Kavya:** 72 = 2³ × 3². A factor can use **0, 1, 2 or 3** twos: **4** choices.
**Priya:** And **0, 1 or 2** threes: **3** choices. **4 × 3 = 12** factors!
**Mr Tan:** **None** is a choice too: **2⁰ = 1**. That's the **+ 1**. Factors = (3 + 1)(2 + 1).
**One:** The plus one... is **ME**! I'm in **every** factor count!
**Paati:** And me? Sixty-four is 2⁶.
**Big Two:** Factors come in **pairs**, but in a **square** one pairs with **itself**: 8 × 8. Only **squares** have an **odd** count.
**Big Two:** A prime has **2** factors. A prime squared, like **49**, has **3**: 1, 7, 49.
**Paati:** Seven factors. Lucky seven. And prime. Tonight I'm collecting everything.

chapters.title: The party saves you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Before the credits, the party would like to save you some marks.
**Banyan:** One. Never leave a **composite** in your answer. 2² × 9 × 5? Split the 9. **Multiply back** to check.
**Hattie:** Two. A **product** of primes means **multiplied**, in index form. Not a list. Not plus signs.
**Big Two:** Three. **Building up** or **breaking down**? Decide first: **LCM** or **HCF**.
**Paati:** Four. Answer the question asked: **7:36 p.m.**, not 36. My sisters were very clear.
**Mr Tan:** Five. **HCF × LCM = a × b** works for **two** numbers only. Never three.
**Ah Boy:** Six. Square roots: halve the **powers**, not the number. I said 882. I was very confident.
**Narrator:** Prime Time will return.
**One:** Big Two! Can I come in **now**?
**Big Two:** Members: **exactly two** factors. You've still got one.
**Paati:** He's not a member. He's my **plus one**.
**Big Two:** ...Go on, then. As a **plus one**.
**One:** I'M IN! I'm in the **club**!
**Big Two:** Still not prime.
